speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I be permitted to offer wholehearted congratulations to the Hamilton Tiger-Cats on winning the Grey cup? I was there rooting for the other side, but Hamilton won; there is no doubt about that. As for the Winnipeg Blue Bombers, we are still very proud of them. In football, as in elections, there is always the next one. Watch out for it.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Leader of ihe Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I had hoped, and I know the hope is shared by many on this side of the house, that the Prime Minister would be informing us about the additional legislation that is to be brought before parliament during this session before we had to deal with the motion extending the time for the consideration of that business. If it would be convenient for the Prime Minister to give us that information, we would be obliged to him.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the other day the Leader of the Opposition asked what additional items of legislation, over and above those already on the order paper, the government hoped would be introduced and considered at this session. The additional items which we have in mind are as follows: An amendment changing the basis for contributions in 96698-109J
respect of unemployment assistance; a bill to authorize a loan to the government of New Brunswick for the Beechwood development and also in that connection, provided an agreement is arrived at between the government of Saskatchewan and the dominion government, the necessary legislation respecting the South Saskatchewan dam and irrigation project.
At the very earliest opportunity I intend to move a motion respecting the rule on closure. There will be a bill dealing with the power program in the Atlantic provinces and also, following negotiation and I hope before the session concludes, the necessary bill to provide adjustment grants to the Atlantic provinces. There are one or two taxation measures which will receive attention and an amendment to the Indian Act to prevent the possibility of Indians who are resident on reservations and were so resident prior to a certain date having their names removed from the band rolls. In the same connection, provided there is time, there will be an amendment to the citizenship act to remove the discrimination that now exists as between natural born and naturalized citizens in connection with the loss of citizenship.
Then there is a very important bill which we realize cannot be considered in full at this time. Indeed, I doubt whether we will have time for any consideration, but the matter has been given very considerable attention. I refer to the new estate tax act. That bill will contain many sections and I feel, with a view to giving members of the house and interested persons across the country an opportunity to give the fullest study to the various sections, that we should go no further than to give the bill first reading. This would enable consideration to be given between the present session and an ensuing session, and as a result of any representations made during the interval further changes might be made in connection with the suggested amendments or changes to the existing law.
I should like to ask a supplementary question. Is there any consideration or legislation intended to increase the pensions of retired civil servants?
No answer?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
I have already stated on a previous occasion that the matter is receiving most careful consideration. There are many details that require to be ironed out

Business of the House
and anomalies that will be created which have made necessary the most careful study of the matter, and as soon as we are in a position to present the legislation covering that matter, parliament of course will have the matter brought before it.

Thank you; we are expecting it.
Mr. Stanley Knowles (Winnipeg North
Centre): I should like to ask a question concerning one item in the list the Prime Minister just gave us. He referred to certain measures having to do with taxation. Would those measures be in lieu of a budget or would they be measures that would grow out of a budget? Would he be more specific about what he had in mind when he made that reference?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
In looking over the
records of parliament throughout the years, I find there have been several occasions, and in particular when second sessions have taken place in the same year, when no budget has been introduced. This was the case in the second session of 1873; in the second session of 1919; in the second session of 1930, which was the first session under the new government. Then it will be recalled also that in December, 1947, there was no budget but there were extensive fiscal changes. Mr. Abbott made the announcement and named special tariff increases, and in implementing them he simply made a motion on going into committee of ways and means.
In so far as changes in the income taxes are concerned, those changes could be made by notice; and in my opinion the few changes that will be made, having regard to the shortage of time available and the fact that this is the second session this year and in the main to the fact that consideration is to be given to the estimates prepared and advanced by the former government, we feel that a formal budget is not necessary at this time.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the members of this party, as we have stated from the beginning of the session, are anxious to co-operate to have the house deal with the business that requires to be dealt with at this time, and we will make no objection to this extension of the hours and even the days of sittings. However, we express the hope that good use will be made of the additional time.
We wish to mention particularly, as I mentioned on Friday, the anxiety of the Canadian public to have brought down at the earliest possible moment the legislation dealing with the fixation of floor prices for agricultural products. We hope that legislation will be brought in at an early date so

it may get the consideration which a matter of that importance deserves under the conditions which exist at the present time.
This subject of taxation is another matter about which there is uncertainty in the public mind which I think is rather detrimental to the economy. Rumours that have circulated in the press have created a situation which has been regarded by some as justification for ceasing production of such things as motor cars which are not being purchased at this time. In view of the possibility of there being a change in the excise tax on motor cars that would make a substantial difference in the price a purchaser would pay, we can all realize that he would be inclined to wait and see whether or not there is going to be that kind of reduction. I would suggest that the government give earnest consideration to removing that uncertainty as early as possible.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) said there would be one or two acts making changes in taxation. I think everyone remembers what was said during the election campaign, and everyone remembers that in the speech from the throne there was a statement that there would be submitted to us for approval changes in certain taxing statutes. There have also been frequent assertions that the promises made during the election campaign would be implemented. I think hon. gentlemen opposite should feel rather complimented that the public should expect that those promises are going to be implemented and should be acting in a manner which shows that they are waiting to see just how far these changes are going to make it more attractive to indulge in certain purchases.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the tremendous amount of work that is yet to be completed in this session of parliament, we are not going to oppose the suggestion that the hours of sitting be extended. We are here to do a job, and we are prepared to sit whatever hours are necessary.
There is one comment about the hours of sitting that I wish to make before I make the comments which I originally rose to give to the house. That comment is this. A rather unusual situation has developed in the proposing of morning sittings, in that this motion proposes morning sittings for Wednesdays, Thursdays, Fridays and Saturdays but not for Mondays and Tuesdays. The reason for that situation is quite clear. This motion has come much earlier than usually happens in a session, and Mondays and Tuesdays are still available either for private

members' resolutions on Mondays or for supply motions on both Mondays and Tuesdays. There is therefore no advantage to the government in asking us to sit Monday and Tuesday mornings so long as we are dealing with matters which are taken up mainly by private members of the house.
I would suggest to the house leader that if this session continues-as it may well do, in view of the tremendous amount of business yet to be done-to the point where the government wishes to ask us to sit Monday and Tuesday mornings as well, when that time comes consideration might be given to leaving Wednesday mornings clear. I think the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) will agree that across the years it has been the practice to leave Wednesday mornings clear for caucuses and other meetings which have to be held. I do not make this request at the moment because we still have Monday and Tuesday mornings clear for these purposes, but I do make that request if the other situation to which I have referred should arise.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the other comment I wish to make is that it seems to me the government should realize that this session is not just, as government spokesmen are so often wont to say, a session for the purpose of cleaning up items left over from the session that met here from January to April for this year. That is an excuse used by the government quite frequently for putting the pressure on us to speed up so far as the consideration of the estimates are concerned.
I think it should be pointed out that the main estimates which are before this house were presented to this session of parliament by the present government. The present government may say that it was the former government which prepared them, but it is the present government which laid them before parliament and it is the present government which is spending the money. Therefore as long as the present government has to take the responsibility for this money this present parliament has the right to discuss those estimates which the government has told us, time and time again, we must rush through and get out of the way so we can get on with legislation.
I find there is also a popular notion abroad -and I might say quite frankly that some of the new members have expressed this notion to me when we chat out in the halls and in the cafeteria-that we are duplicating, so far as estimates are concerned, discussions we had in the last session of parliament. I have checked the records very carefully, and I find that in the January to April session we spent about four days on the estimates of the Post Office Department. We completed those estimates and they are not now before us.
Business of the House
Other than that, the only time we spent on main estimates between January and April of this year consisted of ten minutes on February 22, which we spent on the estimates of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, and one hour on March 7 which we spent on the main estimates of that same department. We spent no other time in the whole of last session on the main estimates which were introduced in the last session and which have been reintroduced in this session.
Some hon. members may have it in their minds that we spent time in the committee of supply on agriculture and one or two other departments. That is true, but that was in relation to supplementary estimates for the year before last. I have checked this very carefully and other members can do the same, but I put it again in this very simple statement: that apart from the post office estimates which were completed and are out of the way, the only time in the whole of last session spent on the main estimates which are now before this parliament was one hour and ten minutes spent on the estimates of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources.
Let no one say that we are duplicating discussion; let no one say that these estimates should be rushed through. Indeed the Prime Minister is the last person who can say that, because on April 11 of last year, in the last week of the old session, he complained, and I shared his complaint, that no opportunity had been given for a critical examination of the estimates.
The Progressive Conservatives, in opposition as they were then, demanded from the former government an assurance when interim supply bills were put through that we would still have our full rights to discuss the main estimates as fully and as completely as we wished.
The government may say that no one is curtailing our rights but I submit, Mr. Speaker, that every time a minister says we should put the estimates through so we can get along with the legislation, every time there is an appeal for co-operation, an attempt is being made to put these things through without that critical examination which the Prime Minister suggested was so important when he spoke from the other side of the house last April.
Mr. Speaker, I should like also to point out by way of opposition to this demand to rush things through that the way things are now going we are likely to go through two sessions of parliament, the one that started in January and ended in April and this one which started in October and will end heaven

Business of the House
knows when, without having had debates on the motion to go into supply on the number of days which the rules entitle us to have in one session.
This is another point concerning which there are some popular misapprehensions. Only today one hon. member told me that we had spent plenty of time on supply motions last session. No, we did not. The Conservatives complained about that, too. We had only one full dress two-day debate on a supply motion in the last session. An amendment was moved to that motion by the then leader of the opposition with regard to the national development policy of the Conservative party. We had that one two-day debate, at the end of which six departments were put into supply.
There were complaints by Conservatives last session that more of these debates were not permitted. As a result of those complaints, during what was the last week of the last session the former government arranged for a one-day supply debate at the end of which no departments were put into supply. It was simply a day's debate as a vehicle to make it possible for the then leader of the opposition to move his amendment having to do with parity prices. Even if you count that day, which was rather perfunctory, we had only three days in the last session for debates on the motion that Mr. Speaker leave the chair for the house to go into committee of supply.
As far as this session is concerned, the matter has been subject to some negotiations through the usual channels. I indicated on Friday at six o'clock that I was a little disturbed over the way certain things which I thought had been agreed to had been upset. We were, for example, to have had a supply motion tomorrow. I am not going to debate that just now, for despite the fact that agreements seem to have been forgotten, we are still prepared to negotiate. But I doubt whether, in fact, at the end of this session we shall come out with more than seven or eight days of debate on the motion that Mr. Speaker do leave the chair for the house to go into committee of supply. If it is seven, plus three of last session, that will only be ten days in two parliamentary sessions. The rule book provides for at least six debates in each session, each of two days, which makes a total of 24 days for two sessions, or twelve days for one session.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that our rights are being curtailed. I say to the government across the way that we have no objection to the suggestion that we work longer hours and try to get along with the business before parliament. But I remind the government

that one of the reasons they are where they are is that the people of Canada became apprehensive about the way in which the Liberal government was pushing parliament around and denying parliament as a whole and private members in particular some of their basic rights. What is being done is not at all like what was done during the pipeline debate, but it is not a long step from pushing parliament around in little ways to doing it in bigger ways.
I admit that the government has done a number of things this session which show respect for parliament. I suggest-I plead-[DOT] that there should not be this attempt to tell parliament that it must not spend time discussing the estimates. Second, an attempt to curtail the right to debate motions that Mr. Speaker leave the chair is an attempt to curtail the rights of private members themselves. These things are part of the rights of parliament, and we are just as entitled to them under a Conservative administration as we felt we were under a Liberal administration.
I point out also, Mr. Speaker, that a number of committees will now be sitting. The external affairs committee has already had one meeting; it is to meet on Tuesday, and has arranged a number of meetings through the next few weeks. The house leader announced on Friday evening at six o'clock that a number of measures would be referred to standing committees of the house. Everyone who has been here before knows how difficult it becomes to do the business of the house and the business of committees when they are meeting concurrently. Let us not have added to that any difficulties so far as arranging the business of the house is concerned.
I say to the house leader, despite the difficulties we have had recently over agreements that have been made, that we are still prepared to negotiate so far as the business of the house is concerned, provided that we can come to agreements and stick to those agreements. But if agreements are to be set aside we shall have no option but to fall back on the rules of the house with regard to supply debates being for two days, with regard to the number of departments that can be put in, and so on.
One other word, Mr. Speaker. A couple of years ago, or was it more, we had a committee on procedure. Everyone knows what went on in that committee. Everyone knows that one of the desires of Mr. Harris, who on that committee, was to cut the number of days for estimates down to 20 per session. The Conservatives would not agree to it; we would not agree to it either.

I ask the Conservatives to remember that. They should not try now to cut two sessions of parliament down to fewer than 20 days for considering estimates that amount to a total of over $5 billion.
I said, Mr. Speaker, that was one other word. There is still another. I am deeply concerned about what the Prime Minister said a few moments ago as to his belief that taxation changes can be made without going through the requirements of our rules so far as the presentation of a budget is concerned. I noted that he had to go back a long way in history to find some examples. Some of them were quite ancient. One was in 1930, when Mr. Bennett came to power. I think some of the things that Mr. Bennett did should be forgotten.
The other example was that of 1947 when Mr. Abbott imposed taxation by radio. I could hardly believe my ears when I heard the Prime Minister quoting that as an example. Those of us who were here will remember the vehemence with which the Conservatives of that day criticized the course taken by Mr. Abbott in proposing tax changes by radio. The present Prime Minister, the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) and the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) were strong in their denunciation of that practice, and so were we.
As a matter of fact it was in connection with that matter, when it was debated later on, that we were able on one occasion in committee of ways and means to defeat the government by a vote on the opposition side that was larger than the vote on the then government side. To complete the story, that result was set aside by an appeal from the ruling made by Mr. Golding, who was then chairman of the committee of ways and means. I recall this, Mr. Speaker, just to remind the Conservatives what they thought when they were in opposition about budgetary changes being made by means of an announcement, and then being put through the house in a way different from what is called for by the rules.
May I tell the Prime Minister that there has been a change in the rules since then. We now have standing order No. 58 which is in different terms from the standing order having to do with the budget prior to 1955. It seems to me that under a proper reading of standing order No. 58, if any budget presentation is being made on proposals for changes in taxation measures, the requirements of standing order 58 will have to obtain. The motion will have to be debatable, and if that is the case it is debatable for a period not exceeding eight days.
Business of the House
Now, I submit that it is possible for us to negotiate the matter of the number of days, provided there is respect for the rules; but if the government is going to say that the rule does not apply, then of course, any basis for negotiation is out the window.
We are concerned about this situation. We think what the country needs today and is entitled to have is not just bills providing for expenditures, bills providing for taxation changes, but a financial statement, an accounting as to where we stand in our national finances. We contend that the government is doing all the things that the present ministers condemned when they were on this side of the house, if it tries to make taxation changes without obeying the rules and having a budget debate, and without making a budget presentation through the Minister of Finance, and hence without letting the house know where the country stands so far as its finances are concerned.
These are procedural matters, Mr. Speaker; these are technical matters. When you talk about private members' days, when you talk about supply motions, when you talk about ways and means, the man on the street doesn't understand them the way the man on the street understood what was happening in the pipe-line debate. And yet, despite all that, I suggest that it is in these things that are wrapped up in the maintenance of the rules and the traditions of parliament that our liberty and democracy are at stake. I hope this government now in power, which so recently was talking about the rules, the traditions and the supremacy of parliament, will not forget those speeches either by pushing parliament around in terms of its business or by denying parliament its right to a budget presentation and its right to debate that presentation if taxation changes are to be proposed.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, as I indicated at the outset, I say we are not opposed to the suggestion that we be asked to sit extra hours to get the business of the house completed in some reasonable time. But let us face the fact that we have before us this session, as I said, estimates amounting to $5 billion. We think they should be given the critical examination that the Prime Minister called for on April 11 this year. Also we have before us a long list of important legislative items, including what amounts to a budget. Parliament should not be rushed. Parliament should be given its opportunity to deal with these matters in the proper parliamentary way.

Mr. Speaker, if with not everything the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said,

Business of the House
with certainly the great bulk of it, I find myself in complete agreement. He has summed up the situation very well indeed. I do hope the government will take into careful consideration what he has said.
I do not intend to repeat the arguments used by the hon. member, except to say this. I think it would have been better if the government had planned to bring in a budget this session. I still think it would be proper and in the interests of the country to bring in a budget. I am firmly convinced that in many parts of our country business remains unsettled very largely because it does not know what the government's financial proposal is to be, and it will remain unsettled until such time as a budget has been brought in and business is given assurance. For these reasons, amongst others, I do hope the government will yet find it possible to bring in a budget and let the members of parliament get their teeth into it.
I am quite sure I can say on behalf of my colleagues here that we are prepared to do everything we possibly can to help the government get the business of this session completed. We are prepared to sit longer hours to get the job done, if that is necessary. We have not wasted too much time. I am quite sure on other occasions there has been a shocking waste of time. I think-and I speak about this parliament, not just the government-this parliament thus far has done a remarkably large amount of work, has got through more work than any parliament I have seen in a good many years.
Because there is a responsible opposition.

Mr. Speaker, when we say we are prepared to go along with the government's proposal to sit longer hours, we do not want them to lose sight of the fact that by this time there ought to be some target date toward which we are aiming for the completion of the work of the session. No target date has yet been set or even suggested. I noticed a statement which shocked me in today's Montreal Gazette under the heading, "Current Session Will Run Into '58." It is a Canadian Press dispatch and reads in part as follows:
. . . informants said today that interparty consultations have come up with this schedule:
1.	An adjournment on Saturday, December 21, until Friday, December 27.
2.	A very brief New Year break, with the M.P.'s just taking off January 1 and going back to work the next day.
3.	Finishing up the sitting before the Liberals start the convention to choose a successor to Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent.
I want it definitely known, Mr. Speaker, that there was no interparty consultation to

that extent with our group, and if a suggestion of that kind had been placed before us we would not have agreed to it by any means. Apparently the government now expects to complete the 26 pieces of legislation that are either on the order paper or were mentioned by the Prime Minister today plus the estimates of the 16 departments that have not been touched, and in addition we are entitled to three supply motions and two private members' days between now and Christmas. It is just utterly fantastic to think we can do justice to that amount of work in the limited time between now and Christmas. If it is fantastic to think we can get through that amount of work between now and Christmas, surely we ought to set some target date beyond Christmas in the new year toward which we can work.
I think the fault of the motion that has been moved by the Minister of Public Works is that it does not mention any target date or suggest to the house when the government would like to get through. Because I feel the motion is lacking in that regard I move that it be amended by adding the following:
provided that the house shall prorogue or adjourn on or before December 21, and shall not reconvene before January 6, 1958.
That motion is seconded by my colleague the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch). I move it for this reason. I think members are entitled to a decent Christmas holiday, and we are not sitting in this parliament for the convenience of eastern members only. If we are going to have a decent Christmas holiday and not skip over the business, I think it should be understood that we will work here as hard as we can until December 21, will take a Christmas holiday from then until January 6, come back at that time and take up the work where we left off and do justice to every piece of legislation that is brought before us, and give members ample opportunity to debate as long as they wish the motions to go into supply and private members' resolutions.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
May I put the amendment. I am in doubt whether it is in order. I should like to have the house consider that point. It is moved by Mr. Low that the motion be amended by adding the following proviso:
provided that the house shall prorogue or adjourn on or before December 21, and shall not reconvene before January 6, 1958.
The motion before the house is one to control the hours of sitting, and whether it is possible by an amendment to enlarge that motion to deal with the time of prorogation or adjournment seems to me very

doubtful. I would think if the amendment attempted to limit this new regime for hours of sitting to the period up to December 21, for example, it would be in order; but to say "provided that the house shall prorogue or adjourn on or before December 21 and shall not reconvene before January 6, 1958" strikes me as attempting to settle by way of an amendment something that has a larger import than that. I wonder whether any hon. member would like to address himself to that subject before I rule on the amendment.
Perhaps the hon. member who moved the amendment would like to restrict it, making the amendment applicable only to the period between now and December 21, in which event I would accept it.
Yes, I would be very glad to have the amendment read in that way.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would think that would be in order as an amendment. The motion now reads "December 4, 1957 and thereafter until the end of this session" and the amendment would be to substitute "until December 21, 1957" for "until the end of this session."

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are gathered here in this parliament under very different circumstances than has been the case in any other parliament since confederation. The objective of the government under these conditions has been to get the business of the country done in the most efficient way possible under all the circumstances. We have tried to co-operate with the members of the three parties who happen to be in opposition and to date, as the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) has so truly said, great progress has been made. Many measures have been passed. In an ordinary session that would not have been the case; we would not have made the progress which has been made to date.
We must remember that in the background there is the fact that we are finishing up the business for the year 1957. Surely my hon. friends are not suggesting that we should be going further and doing some of the business for 1958. Yet that is the direction in which some of the arguments advanced by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and the hon. member for Peace River would lead. I am sure everyone in the house is aiming primarily at getting the business done, and under all the conditions I suggest there cannot be very much objection taken to having the house sit these extra hours.
No one is asking that there be any cutting down of the actual discussion. I know just as well as anyone else who has been here for any period of years that the more you suggest
Business of the House
to members that they cut down discussion the longer they are going to take. That, of course, is true of some more than of others.
Let the hon. gentleman speak for himself.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Anyone who wishes to talk during these extended hours is, of course, free to do so. I have no doubt advantage will be taken of that opportunity. We may not save any time at all by adding these extra hours if a sufficient number of members look upon this change as an opportunity to do more talking. But we are trying to do the business of the country, and to get it finished by the end of the year. This suggestion that members cannot sit at all during the Christmas holidays, that they have to go home and stay for two or three weeks, does not do justice to the spirit in which the members of the House of Commons are here. We were elected not to run home for long holidays but to do the business of the country.

Will the minister permit a question? I am in agreement with the extended sittings, but I understood the minister to say we had to finish the estimates this year. Is it not a fact that the financial year ends March 31, not December 31?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I said we are trying to finish the business of 1957 in 1957. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar knows very well that that business for 1957 includes the estimates. Surely he is not arguing that we should continue a discussion of the estimates until March 31, 1958?
We could.

May I ask the minister a question. Is the minister implying that this house should go along with him and not question what the government is asking if that requires another month or six weeks in 1958 to finish up the business of this session?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I am not asking the house to go along with me, but I do suggest that the members of the house should try to get the business for 1957 finished in 1957, or as soon thereafter as possible.
The Leader of the Opposition asked us about two items of legislation. One was the proposal to provide guaranteed prices for certain agricultural commodities. He expressed the hope that this measure would be brought up for debate at an early date. As the right hon. gentleman knows, I announced on Friday that that measure would be on the list for tomorrow.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
on the list.

Business of the House

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: The other resolutions should not take very long. If my hon. friends want to take three or four hours on each one, that is another matter.
Closure.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
That is the plan of the government, to bring this resolution on for consideration tomorrow.
Then the right hon. gentleman also asked about any legislation which would change the excise tax on automobiles. Any change of this nature in a taxation measure will be announced just as quickly as possible. We realize the importance of having such an announcement made, and I can assure the right hon. gentleman that it will be made just as quickly as we can possibly do so.
Then the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre made a statement which was very encouraging to me. He said the government was trying to push parliament around. I do not suppose there ever was a government of Canada that was in such danger of being pushed around itself as the present one is. If we have at least created the impression that we are able to push him and his colleagues around, let alone push around the other opposition parties, then we have not been doing too badly. However, I can assure him that the last thing we have in mind is to push anybody around. We are just as much interested in the rights of parliament as we ever were, just as much interested as my hon. friend and his colleagues. We intend to show every respect for parliament and all the wonderful things for which it stands.
I do not believe, really, Mr. Speaker, that we can be accused of trying to sabotage parliament by anything we have done to date. We intend to carry on in the same way during the remaining days of this parliament. We will try to respect the wishes of all three opposition parties, and try to work out a plan for doing the business of the house which will meet the convenience of all of the members, including the new members of the house. In the meantime I do ask for support for our original motion. We do not believe it is the responsibility of the Social Credit party, or any other of the opposition parties, to decide just when parliament is to be prorogued or just when it is to be adjourned. Those decisions are the responsibility of the government.
No, the responsibility of parliament.

There is one very good way to settle that. If the members of the house are not prepared to accept our recommendation

speechtext: Another threat.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: This, too, is part of our parliamentary procedure, and we shall be very happy to abide by the result.

Does the Canadian Press despatch carried by the Gazette on its front page represent the plans of the government, when it says very definitely that well-informed people have said that is what the government intends to do? That is the first question.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: When the government, Mr. Speaker, makes an announcement, it does not make it to the press.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: What about T.V.?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader

Innocents abroad.

It was merely a friendly

speakeroldname: Mr. F. G. J. Hahn (New Westminster):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I find myself in the position of my name having been brought into this discussion in so far as a decision is concerned as to on what dates we had determined or decided the house might adjourn and be recalled. I must say that while there was some discussion with respect to the possibility, the only intimation I had was that we would probably be recalled the day after Christmas.
I can appreciate the position of the house leader with respect to this matter, because he has certainly consulted with me frequently, has tried to bring me up to date in every way possible, and has discussed this party's viewpoint as presented by me so we could possibly come to some agreement. But
Business of the House
up to this time I must admit I had not definitely had the date of recalling the house drawn to my attention, nor was it suggested that December 21 would be the date when we would recess. It had rather been intimated that we would sit up to Christmas and be recalled the day after Christmas. The house leader might have been under the impression that he had discussed the matter with me, but I do not recall those particular dates being mentioned.

As has
already been said on behalf of this group, Mr. Speaker, we certainly have no objection to increased hours of sitting of the house. We realize that there is before parliament a great deal of business that must be dealt with. However, I am not at all satisfied that the government is giving to the various measures the kind of priority that should be given. With great deference to the Minister of Public Works, I suggest that to say that the resolution which would establish support prices for agricultural products is actually in fact listed for tomorrow, when it is listed in seventh place, is not to say something that has any great merit or any great basis in realism.
If the government were anxious that this legislation, which has been demanded by the official opposition and which this group has requested be brought forward at an early date, and which I am certain would have the support of members of the Social Credit group-when in response to this unanimous request by the three opposition parties the government say "We listed it for Tuesday but we listed it for seventh place," I would suggest that is putting a gun to the heads of members who are interested in the other legislation. I refer to the other six items that have been listed.
I therefore make this request, namely that the government list this legislation first for tomorrow, and we will see how we can expedite it. Some of my colleagues have suggested to me that if the government would be prepared to do that we might be prepared to sit tomorrow morning to deal with this legislation affecting agricultural producers.
What may be happening, Mr. Speaker, is this. The government, by delaying the passing of this legislation-and this is the best you can say for it-is in fact taking away a good deal of money that might otherwise accrue to the producers who are marketing products that might be affected by the resolution. Of course if that is not the case then there is not too much in the resolution. But it seems to me a shame, since the government has been in office since June 21, that

Business of the House
there should be so much delay in bringing forward what we all understand to be an emergency measure.
No one can say that parliament-and in this I include all members of parliament-did not pass with great expedition the various pieces of legislation which the government itself listed as emergency legislation. This therefore is the first thing, I suggest, that the government should be giving consideration to.
I am not sufficient of an authority to know the technicalities with regard to bringing in a budget in a given session or not bringing in a budget, but it seems to me to be a very unsatisfactory state of affairs that because the government is playing coy as to its policy with regard to the excise tax on automobiles, we should have this further large number of persons added to the unemployment rolls in this country. Why does not the government make a statement now as to its position with regard to this suggested change in the excise tax on automobiles? I think it is a mistake that the government should leave this thing suspended for so long, thereby daily adding to the unemployment rolls in this country.
We all hope, of course, that there will be a cut in the excise tax. We hope the government will bring in a budget immediately. But I think this is the kind of problem that should be dealt with so this unemployment, if it is unnecessary as far as the automobile industry is concerned, is not continued. I can understand the position of prospective automobile purchasers in this country. They do not want to risk any chance of paying more than would be the ordinary price if they purchase an automobile now in advance of any prospective reduction. It would seem to me that this is just an ordinary thing that should be done.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I was just going to remind the hon. member that we are dealing with hours of sitting, and that we should not get into discussion of business to come before the house.

Mr. Speaker, I would think I was making a comment on the statement made by the Leader of the Opposition. As far as expediting the business of the house is concerned, I think we are in favour of it. A good deal of legislation has been announced that we shall have to deal with during the current session. As the Prime Minister stated that legislation that we would have to deal with this session it seemed to me there was one major omission, and that was legislation which would provide for payments under the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act on behalf of mental
[Mr. Argue.!
and tuberculosis patients. The second obvious thing was an announcement which would make possible the coming into effect of the hospital insurance provisions at an early date.
I should like to say to the government that it is not compelled at every opportunity to say that if we want to vote for an adjournment, vote for the motion or vote against it, we face the possibility of an election.
There seems to be quite a desire on the part of the government to get defeated on any kind of a motion it can at the earliest possible date. It seems to me the government would be in a much better position if it would take the constructive suggestions advanced by the members of the various opposition parties as to what should be given priority in the way of very necessary legislation.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall try to keep to the motion which is before the house, but I would like to make one or two points in connection with what the leader of the government stated a moment ago.
It is true that certain discussions took place between us in connection with a general plan to deal with the business of the house from that time, which was at least a month ago, until the Christmas recess. The plan which was submitted appeared to me to be in order in so far as its general terms were concerned, but I do want to make it quite clear that at no time was there any agreement as between us in connection with any plan such as that announced in this morning's Gazette. I want to dissociate myself from any understanding or any agreement in so far as that is concerned.
As the leader of our party has said, I was not here on Thursday or Friday-

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, I said there was no agreement with anybody, but that it was simply a matter of discussion.

speechtext:
Well, that was not even discussed. I think my hon. friend indicated that this group had been told something about the plan. I want to make it quite clear that I, for one, was not consulted about this.
There are, however, one or two other points with which I would like to deal in speaking to this motion and to the amendment. The leader of the house has said that we are gathered here in unprecedented circumstances. Well, I do not think the circumstances are so unprecedented. After all, there have been two sessions within a 12-month period before, and the responsibility of the government is to bring in the estimates,

the legislation and any other business. It therefore does not seem to me that there is anything unprecedented about the circumstances in which we find ourselves.
Our leader a moment ago asked the Prime Minister for the intended legislation, other than that on the order paper before us now, for the remainder of the session, and I am just wondering if it is the intention of the government to get through all of this business before the end of this year. After all, there are on this list some measures which it seems to me have no urgency, and certainly others-for instance, that dealing with closure-which could be of such a contentious nature as to take a great deal of the time of the house.
That being the case, I wonder how it is going to be possible that all this legislation now on the order paper, and that now announced by the Prime Minister, could get through in that time. We have from now until the Christmas recess, and so I ask this question with all deference. Is it really the intention of the government to get through with the business of the house, or is it inviting a vote of non-confidence so as to provide a reason to go before the country?
Those are the considerations which come to my mind at this time; and while we will facilitate the business of the house, as my leader has said, there is one thing I hope we will not be asked to do, and that is to put some of these measures through with such haste that it will be impossible to consider them seriously in the manner in which they should be considered, at least on second reading. Those are the observations I have to make on this motion.

As the leader of this group has mentioned, Mr. Speaker, we are prepared to adopt the hours of sitting mentioned in this motion, but I think the leader of the house should be prepared to at least be reasonable. He must admit that the proposal as it now stands is fantastic. He is saying the times we shall sit in this house until the end of the session, and if there was any possibility of making the end of the session before Christmas I would agree with the reasonableness of this motion. But the leader of the house knows very well that there is no possibility of completing the business of the house before us at the present time by December 21. Seventeen days left, 26 pieces of legislation, 15 departments, three supply motions and two private members' days. For anybody to suggest that all this could be completed before Christmas, as I say, is fantastic.

Irresponsible.
Business of the House Mr. Quelch: If, on the other hand, we are going to come back after Christmas-and undoubtebly we will have to do so in order to complete this legislation-is it necessary that we should sit this kind of hours for an unlimited time in order to complete this legislation, especially when the closure motion is among the measures? Mind you, closure is still in force, and the house leader may figure that his party will be able to use closure, get it through, and then do away with it.
That's a hot one.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I declare the amendment lost. The question is-

Mr. Speaker, before you put the motion I should like to have a word. I did not speak on the main motion; it was my colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), who dealt with it. I want to say this to the government. Because of the condition that exists in this house at the present time the government would be well advised to do what was done when a government since I have been here had a very narrow majority. I am referring to the period between 1945 and 1949, when, from time to time in the discussions of the business of the house, the leaders and the whips of the opposition parties were called into consultation. They might come to some agreement without a long discussion of this description. Since the beginning of this session there has been no consultation. The leader of the house from time to time has seen members of the opposition groups and has said what the government intends to do. That, in reality, is not the kind of consultation that there should be under these circumstances. We are willing to sit all the hours that are necessary to do the business of this house.
There is a tremendous list of legislation now. I am amazed at the number of items


that were added this afternoon. Some of them are of the utmost importance. I want to say to the government that some attempts should be made to organize the discussion of this legislation. We should try to get the legislation through. The estimates should also be dealt with by this house; but I want to say to the government again that the estimates we are now discussing are not the estimates up to December 31, 1957. These are estimates up to March 31 of next year and consequently we should be able to have ample time to discuss them. I do not think it is the function-that is perhaps why we did not vote with the Social Credit group-of either the opposition or the government simply to say that this is what we are going to do and have done with it. There should be consultation. I think we should try to get consultation-
I tried to get consultation.

The leader of the Social Credit group was laying something down to the house. I think it would be far better if the government took the attitude of consultation. Let us organize the discussion of this legislation, if we can. Some of the legislation should go through immediately. Farm legislation has been mentioned several times this afternoon and then, of course, the financial position of the country should be known.
These are matters of the utmost concern to this parliament and they should take priority over everything else. The people of this country have a right to know-particularly if there is any intention on the part of the government to call an election in the near future-the financial position of this country and what the legislation that we have adopted this session means to the finances of this country. We have added these commitments which we support. I think the people of the country have the right to know above all things what the financial condition of this country is and we should not leave here until we know. That means, of course, that a budget should be brought down before this session winds up.
I want to make a plea to the government so that we may not have the kind of discussion we have had this afternoon, and so we may have consultation to try to get something agreed upon by the parties in regard to legislation and proceed with the estimates and give them a thorough going over, which they deserve. Incidentally, we owe that to those who sent us here.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, pursuant to standing order 26 I beg leave to move the adjournment of the house for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance. Your Honour will note that the mover of such a motion must, pursuant to subsection 3 of standing order 26, hand to Your Honour a written statement setting out the matter which he proposes to discuss as a matter of urgent public importance. That I have done and I now await your ruling as to my right to raise this matter.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: What is the matter of urgent public importance?

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: I followed strictly the rules set out in standing order 26. I have no objection to stating what Your Honour now has, namely that there is a matter of urgent public importance in our country arising out of the closing of automobile plants resulting in the lay-off of thousands of automobile workers for an indefinite period.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Is that all you have got to say?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
The urgent matter of public importance which is the subject of this motion, as I understand it, relates to the closing or shutting down in whole or in part of automobile plants in Canada and the threatened closing of automobile plants.
While I think the house will agree that this is a matter of public importance and public interest, X wonder whether any hon. members would care, before I make the decision which it is my duty to make, to address themselves to the question of the responsibility of the government in the matter and the question of urgency of debate
Labour Conditions
which, after all, is the important question I have to decide. It is not that the matter itself is of urgent public importance, as most matters before the house are, but whether it is a matter of urgency of debate, assuming that it is of urgent public importance. Perhaps the proposer would say a word.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if I may have the floor for a minute, I think we at least ought to know the wording of the motion so that we can speak to it. We have always had that courtesy shown before.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:

In accordance with this standing order-
That is standing order No. 26.
-I herewith submit a statement of the matter to be discussed. The matter of urgent public importance which I propose to raise has to do with the fact that two large automobile companies in Canada, employing thousands of workers, have closed their doors for an indefinite period and another large company, in fact, the largest, proposes to shut its doors tomorrow or the next day.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Is there not an additional paragraph to the effect that the confusion was created by the announcement respecting the excise tax on automobiles?

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26

I wish to address you now, Mr. Speaker. I would call your attention to subsection 3 of standing order 26 which is explicit in this matter. Every move I have taken is in accordance with the rules, as Your Honour well knows. Subsection 3 is in these words:
He then hands a written statement of the matter proposed to be discussed to Mr. Speaker, who, if he thinks it in order, and of urgent public importance, reads it out and asks whether the member has the leave of the house.
The grounds for this motion are another matter and they have been properly stated under the rules but I submit in the wrong context by the hon. member for Vancouver East. There is this large-scale lay-off which was announced by three automobile companies on Saturday last, as contained in the Saturday edition of the Globe and Mail, as the result of hesitation in the tax policy of the administration, clarification of which policy has been sought by representatives of the automobile industry, the factory workers and members of this house over a period beginning almost at the opening of this session of parliament.

Order. I do not want the

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
should like to address myself to the question that is of greatest concern to Your Honour, namely whether there is urgency of debate with respect to this matter. Before I do so, perhaps I might point out to the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) that his motion, in the form in which he presented it to the house, was to say the least incomplete. He quotes subsection 3 of standing order 26. I wonder whether he read subsection 2, which comes before subsection 3. It says:
The member desiring to make such a motion rises in his place, asks leave to move the adjournment of the house for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, and states the matter.
The hon. member for Essex East forgot to state the matter. The fact that he sent notice to Your Honour in advance does not mean that he has complied with the requirement of the last four words of subsection 2 of standing order 26.
I would also draw the attention of the hon. member for Essex East to page 323 of Beauchesne's third edition. At the bottom of that page there is an instruction as to how to draft a motion of this kind. True, in Beauchesne's third edition, the reference is to standing order 31 but that was the number before the last revision of the rules and

standing order 26 in today's rules is the same as standing order 31 was under the old rules.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: What page?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Page 323 of Beauchesne, third edition. The instruction reads:
The member, from his place in the house, says: "Mr. Speaker, I ask leave to move the adjournment of the house under standing order 31-"
Now standing order 26.
"-for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely" (here describe the question to be debated). He then hands a written statement of the matter to be discussed to the Speaker who, having read it to the house, puts the question: "Has the hon. member leave to proceed?"
Now, if the hon. member for Essex East did not know where to find that in the rule book, he could have looked up last Friday's Hansard and copied the form of the motion put by my colleague the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue). I realize that the hon. member for Essex East, who has been in parliament for a long time, has not had any experience with this type of motion. He should have consulted some of us on this side who have had lots of experience in opposition. However, I gather Your Honour does not want to make an issue out of the incomplete form of the motion, for you can easily write in the words the hon. member for Essex East had in mind.
This leaves us with the more important and serious question of the urgency of debate. I support very strongly and wholeheartedly the proposition that there is urgency of debate. May I point out that in doing so I am asking the house to take up more time on this private members' Monday which otherwise would have been devoted to a motion standing in my name, so the impartiality of the position I am taking is obvious. It has been ruled many times, Mr. Speaker, that urgency of debate rather than just the urgency of the situation is the criterion. There is no argument about the urgency of the situation. Indeed, Your Honour has admitted that. The fact is employees are being laid off and there are other things happening that are upsetting the country in regard to this situation.
What about urgency of debate? The fact is that during the whole of this session we have been trying to get a statement from the government regarding its plans with respect to a budget. Up until today, we have not been able to get any kind of statement at all. All of the answers from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) have been, to put it politely, evasive. Even today the statement of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker)

still leaves a great deal of uncertainty as to taxation changes, and that uncertainty is on two counts.
On the one hand, we do not know when they are coming, and I submit that is a matter that should be debated today because if there has been confusion in the automobile industry in the last few days there will be more confusion after the statement made today, with no follow-up as to when these measures are to be introduced. There is uncertainty as to whether the taxation measures to be introduced by the government will include changes in the excise tax so far as automobiles are concerned. There is also uncertainty as to the government's intention regarding the way this matter is to be introduced. Is there to be a budget debate or not? Are there to be resolutions that will be passed by parliament or just resolutions, notice of which will be given to parliament? All of this is in such a state of confusion, both so far as parliament is concerned and so far as the automobile industry and its employees are concerned, that it seems to me there is one thing that is required today-I will even say it is more important than debating my motion-and that is a debate in this house to find out where we stand in relation to the introduction of any measures affecting the exise tax on automobiles.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, despite the comments I made regarding the incompleteness of the form of the motion presented by the hon. member for Essex East, I hope you will consider my contention that there is not only urgency so far as the situation is concerned, with men losing their jobs, but there is urgency of debate. This matter should be discussed and cleared up in the House of Commons today.

However, as the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) has pointed out, this situation is not confined to merely those centres where automobiles are manufactured in this country. The very interdependence of our economy suggests, of course, that the situation is much more widespread in this particular instance, than a mere recital of the number of men who may be out of work in the city of Windsor, in the city of Oshawa or any other centres, such as Hamilton, where automobiles are manufactured.
One has to take into account that the situation affects the dealers in automobiles all over this country and in every community; one has to consider the effect on a score of subsidiary plants, not only in my own community but in other communities of Canada which are entirely dependent upon the manufacture of automobiles.
This, therefore, is by no means a local question or one of local consideration; this is

a national matter and I do not argue for one moment that if the situation was confined to my own city that would preclude any hon. member from raising this particular matter but, to give emphasis to the nature of the problem about which we complain, I join with the hon. member for Bow River in indicating the nationwide character of the problem.
Now I want to be fair in a matter of this importance and I would not suggest that this is the first time unemployment has occurred within recent months or within a recent period in the automobile industry; that would be neither a fair argument nor would it be a responsible one, and I do not think I am inclined to make irresponsible arguments in support of a case in this house. Now I wish to refer to a matter which I regret having to raise since the hon. the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), undoubtedly for good reasons, is not in his seat but I have to weigh the convenience of the hon. minister and the interests of my constituents, so I think he will not criticize me, in this instance at any rate, if I prefer the welfare of my constituents to his convenience. I indicated in my question that there was some concern about his refusal or his inability to see the representatives of that industry on the next day. The minister replied that he had already seen them several weeks before. He also indicated that he had seen the dealers and that he was aware of the nature of the problems confronting the automobile industry. He would give no commitment however as to whether or not he would see them. There may have been good reasons why the government did not call parliament early enough, but certainly one of the reasons for the present situation is that parliament was not called sufficiently early to deal with these problems. The second reason is this. I would remind my hon. friends of the Liberal party that when we moved an amendment in reply to the address we regretted that inflation and unemployment were not mentioned in the speech from the throne. My Liberal friends did not support us in that contention in supporting the amendment which we moved.
However, this situation has arisen because of another reason. The other reason is we have had no budget. This doubt that has arisen in the public mind and in the mind of the industry which is resulting in such disastrous unemployment in Windsor, in Oshawa, in Hamilton would not have arisen. automobile industry in the manufacturing of parts, tires and other equipment for the automobile industry. Now, of course, those citizens will feel the pinch again because of unemployment and lay-offs in the automobile industry. When I was in Brantford two or three weeks ago I was told by the mayor that not so many years ago there were 15,000 men employed in the agricultural implement industry in that city. When I was there three weeks ago there were
7,000	employed in that same industry, and some of them had been transferred from the agricultural industry to manufacturing parts for automobiles.
One can see, therefore, that this matter is not the concern only of Essex East. This does not concern only Windsor; it does not concern only Oshawa or Hamilton, it concerns a very large number of other places in this country today. In view of the dangerous level to which unemployment has already risen in Canada, the fact that this confusion has arisen over whether or not the excise tax is going to be reduced from 10 per cent to 5 per cent or is to be wiped out is an aggravation of that unemployment situation.
So I am rising this afternoon to support the contention of the hon. member for Essex East. But there again, in view of the financial situation and in view of the position of other industries in this country, I think the question of whether taxes are to be lowered or raised, whether through income tax reductions more purchasing power is given whereby people may buy more things to help alleviate the unemployment situation and whether this tax is going to be reduced or eliminated, should be included in a review of the financial situation in this country by means of a budget. I do not think it is satisfactory for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) to rise in his place perhaps tomorrow or next week and make some announcement.
I want to say to the government that I do not know how the rumour got abroad that a reduction was going to be made in the excise tax. Whether or not there was a leak, I do not know. But because that story appeared in a paper that is regarded as being very close to the present administration, namely the Toronto Telegram, great credence was given to it. There may be other factors in this situation also, of which some of us may not be unaware. When the story appeared in the press it may have alerted the automobile industry. The management and the owners of the automobile industry might have considered that at last they had been handed

a very good lever by means of which to get rid of this tax and to put the government thoroughly on the spot in relation to it. I do not think we can discount that possibility. But whether or not that was the intention of the management, it is not the management that will suffer. It is the workers in the industry who are going to suffer.
As far as I am concerned, I am not interested in the high profits of General Motors, Ford or Chrysler or in the payment of big bonuses to the management of those automobile organizations. I am interested in the condition of the men and women who work in that industry. They are out of work today and are threatened with more unemployment unless something is done. I recall that the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) in his radio address on November 8 deprecated our talking about unemployment, said that warning of the dangers of unemployment was a dangerous course to follow and one which, he suggested, could lead to a depression.
We are not suggesting that the unemployment in this one industry is leading to a recession or depression but we are concerned with the general condition across the country. The more unemployment we have in the automobile industry, the larger are the figures which are already startling. The statistics that we have indicate the seriousness of the problem, to which unemployment in the automobile industry is adding. Unplaced applicants in October of this year, 1957, according to the latest figures, numbered 280,000 compared with 160,000 a year ago, a figure higher than the figure in October, 1954 when we were entering the bad winter of 1954-55. Of course it was not an opposition member who predicted that if unemployment continued to develop as it has been developing by the spring of next year we might have 750,000 people seeking work across this country. It was said by an official of the government. At a time when we are all worried over the condition of the working people in the various industries in this country this situation develops and I say that the government should clear it up and do so as rapidly as possible.
I blame the government for not bringing down a budget this autumn and allowing the people of Canada to know precisely what the financial condition of this country is, what the new taxation proposals were, whether they intend to reduce certain taxes, including income taxes, raise the exemption or what-have-you, in order that more purchasing power might be put in the hands of the people to help to buy the goods that industry

is producing. Because those goods cannot be sold unemployment is developing in those industries. As far as the automobile industry is concerned, probably sales were dropping. I think the automobile industry in this country-and we are not discussing that industry except in so far as it affects unemployment-has gone crazy in the production of comparatively high priced cars.

What I was proceeding to say when I was interrupted by the point of order, Mr. Speaker-which point of order was properly taken, I might say, and I have no objection to being interrupted on that account because I think in the future those hon. members who want to discuss matters of urgent public importance will see that they fulfil the requirements of the rule book.
I have been a member of this house for 22 years and this is the first time this point has been raised in the manner in which it was raised this afternoon. I do not recall any occasion quite like it. However, the debate has proceeded. I was saying that in view of the growing unemployment situation, the fact that lay-off announcements have been made by the automobile companies indicates how necessary it is for the government to take immediate action to resolve this situation. Mr. Walker, the president of General Motors of Canada, said the Oshawa plant will be shut down Monday and Tuesday, that is today and tomorrow and all overtime work will be eliminated immediately. This will mean that some 16,400 men in Oshawa alone will be affected, apart altogether from the McKinnon industries at St. Catharines and the other industries making parts for General Motors plant at Oshawa and which as I have said spread right out into the country.
Chrysler did the same thing and said:
-the production cuts were scheduled when "widely-circulated but unsubstantiated news reports stated that a reduction in the excise tax is imminent. The effect of this report has been to bring a complete halt to the shipment of cars from Canadian manufacturers to the dealers."
Dealers on another occasion were caught when a sudden reduction was made in the excise tax and no adequate compensation was provided for the losses they sustained thereafter. I remember, in travelling around my own constituency shortly after the session in which that was done, that I found automobile dealers who were in very difficult circumstances because of the manner in which the reduction in the tax had to be absorbed by the dealers and which the company did not absorb.
To continue my quotation the president of General Motors said:
A decision concerning further shutdowns will be made as soon as more is known about the government's specific plan regarding excise tax costs.
Ford said it will continue with its early cutback program and plans no further reductions because of the decision of the other two companies.

And since that time Mr. Clifford Pilkey, president of Local 222, United Automobile Workers said that:
Protests have been sent to Finance Minister Fleming and Labour Minister Starr.
It is really peculiar that a company which has been hiring so many extra men recently should close down because of newspaper reports or other information that the excise tax is to be reduced.
Mr. Pilkey said: ''General Motors have reacted like the stock market would to General Eisenhower's illness."
That is true, as I said earlier. I think that probably the management of some of these companies are very anxious indeed to use this as a lever to get rid of a tax for whose elimination they have been asking for some considerable time. As I say, while I have no sympathy with the people who have been receiving large bonuses-with the executives of these corporations-I have every sympathy for the men and women who are perhaps being used as pawns in an endeavour to get rid of a tax. I hope the government will make an announcement. There is only one thing for the government to do now; it has been put squarely on the spot, and it must announce either that the tax has been reduced to 5 per cent or that it has been eliminated altogether.

My point is that because of the unemployment situation which has arisen, and because of the reports which have appeared in the papers, the government should make some immediate announcement and say either that it is going to do nothing with regard to this tax or that it is going to eliminate it altogether. If the government is going to reduce it by 5 per cent, as the newspaper reports indicate, it should make a speedy announcement. I ask this not on behalf of the shareholders or the management of the industry but on behalf of the working men and women whose jobs in that industry are adversely affected, and on behalf of many men and women in other parts of Canada whose livelihood and employment would be affected if this question is not settled immediately. Of course, this question is not limited to those directly concerned with the industry itself, it stems back to the steel industry, because rolled steel is used largely in the automobile industry, and some of our steel plants are looking for outlets for their rolled steel and so on.
Thus, Mr. Speaker, this is a serious matter. The hon. member for Essex East was well advised to bring this matter up today, and I am hopeful that we shall get an announcement from the government. I would remind the Prime Minister that on one occasion a former minister of finance made an announcement not in this house but over the radio, and that announcement was approved later on by this House of Commons by the other place and, thereby, by the parliament of Canada. So I appeal for an immediate announcement as to what the government intends to do, either to continue the tax, which I hope it will not do, reduce it to 5 per cent or, better still, eliminate it altogether.
