Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) is not here and I am prepared to say a few words in connection with

this debate. We have heard today, and we are well aware of the fact, that the problem of unemployment is of nationwide concern. The cities of Windsor and Hamilton have been mentioned, in which places there are a large number of people who work in the automobile industry and who are now out of employment. I understand that approximately 16,000 people are affected. This is a very serious situation. It is not only the workers in this industry who are affected but other people as well who rely directly and indirectly upon the industry for a livelihood.
I personally have received a telegram from various members of the Penticton motor dealers association, which telegram urges me to do everything possible to arrange protection for dealers who have new automobiles in stock and en route in the event a reduction in tax is decided upon. It suggests that there should be a plan whereby dealers could be assured of a rebate on all new cars on hand unsold and unused at the time of the change.
As I said before, this matter is of very serious concern to the nation, and it would seem that the government should at this time declare its intention one way or the other whether the present excise tax is to stay as it is or to be reduced. In addition, I would say further that ever since the house opened on October 14 last questions have been asked by members of the opposition parties as to when the government proposes to bring down a budget and so far there is no indication one way or the other in that respect. I feel that we as members of parliament should know what the nature of the income and expenses is expected to be. Accordingly, I urge the government to give every consideration to the problem that is now facing the people of this country.

speakeroldname: Hon. George C. Nowlan (Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
The matter raised this afternoon by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) did not cover the whole panoply of unemployment but was specifically directed toward unemployment in certain industries.	He referred more or less
euphemistically to certain things which might be done to correct that situation. Since the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary (Mr. Christian), who has just taken his seat, also made direct reference to the matter of excise tax on automobiles I thought that for a moment or two I should perhaps deal with that situation within the scope of this debate because I know that the hon. gentleman opposite who moved this motion is not one of the Snow White and Seven Dwarfs, living in a state of fantasy, but is dealing specifically 96698-111
Labour Conditions
with this problem although trying to keep within the rules by avoiding any direct reference to it.
What is there, Mr. Speaker, that distinguishes this situation from other situations in other years? This parliament met on the 14th day of October. We are now in the second day of December and we have been here for a matter of one month and two weeks. We are told that owing to some delay in making some announcement this country is facing a very serious situation. It is a story, Mr. Speaker, which is not entirely original at this time; it is one which many of us have heard before. What distinguishes it? Can we tell this, from other years? Well, we are told that there was one newspaper story. In other years during which many of us have been here there have been scores of newspaper stories speculating on what might be done by the Minister of Finance on a certain unknown date, in a certain indefinite time in the future, and I do not know that the country went entirely to wrack and ruin because of this large number of newspaper stories speculating on what Speaker, how much importance we can attach to that story, or how much should be attached to the suggestion of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) as to what use could be made of that story to hold a club over the head of this government at this time? But if any people in this country-certainly not in this house; I would not think of that-think they can use a newspaper story to wield a club over the head of the government, then they are certainly sadly mistaken.
What else are we told? We are told that there is unemployment in the country at the present time, serious unemployment, and that it is a most tragic thing that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) has not yet made his announcement with respect to whatever the matter may be to which the hon. member for Essex East made reference this afternoon. Everyone knows, Mr. Speaker, that the unemployment of one man is a tragedy to that family and the unemployment of 100, 1,000 or 10,000 is a tragedy to all those directly concerned and to many others. It is not for me to deal with unemployment figures. My colleague, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr), can deal with those most effectively. But I suggest in all seriousness that to state that the degree of unemployment at this time is such as to compel the government to take action which has never been taken before and make premature disclosures of budget matters is absolutely not being realistic.
When the people who used to be on the other side of the house, some of whom are

Labour Conditions
now on this side, used to talk about unemployment the right hon. gentleman who was seated to the right of where the former prime minister sits tonight used to get up and bark and say, "Have you lost your faith in Canada? I have got faith in Canada." He would deal with the matter in that way. I think he deserved credit for that. Have the car manufacturers of this country lost faith in Canada? Have the car dealers lost faith in Canada? Have hon. gentlemen opposite lost faith in Canada? Surely not. Certainly their record in the past would not suggest that because just before I came downstairs tonight I happened to look up the dates on which budgets were brought down by the preceding administration, particularly for the year 1955 when we did have a very substantial degree of unemployment as the winter went on, in fact, the highest degree in our history.
At that time the then minister of finance reduced the excise tax on automobiles by one-third, bringing it down from 15 per cent to 10 per cent. No disclosure was made. No statement was made. There were no cries to heaven in the newspapers about the threat of a disaster or the complete collapse of a ministry. In 1955 parliament met on the 7th day of January and the buget was brought down on the 5th day of April. January, February and March went by, three months of the greatest unemployment this country had ever known. On the 5th of April the budget was brought down and included in it was a reduction of the excise tax on automobiles by one-third.
Yet it is being suggested here that this government in some way is contributing to unemployment, is creating something of a disaster, by refusing to deal with the matter realistically, by refusing to deal with it prematurely and at the whim and behest of a newspaper story such as that. The matter of tax reduction is, of course, one which is in the hands of the Minister of Finance. He makes the disclosures. He makes his recommendations to the cabinet and then in turn to the House of Commons. In 1957 the house opened on January 8 and the budget was brought down on March 14. In 1956 parliament opened on January 10 and the budget was brought down on March 20, and in 1955, as I said, which was the worst year of all for unemployment, over three months elapsed before the budget was brought down.
You know, Mr. Speaker, that old adage about those who came to scoff remained to pray certainly applies to those who are now in the opposition. When they were in the government they scoffed at the pleas

of the then opposition to take some action with respect to those things about which they are now praying. What the government proposes to do with respect to taxation will, of course, be announced by the Minister of Finance at the proper time and in that way we will be following the practice which has been laid down ever since confederation.
I think some special reference should be made to legislation which was passed last year by this parliament. We hear rumours and reports-some people were in my office today -of almost a sit-down strike between the dealers and the manufacturers and that a very serious crisis is developing between them. It is not for us to deal with matters of trade between the people engaged in that tremendous business. I am sure they are competent and able and can solve their own differences.
But when anyone suggests it is the fault of the government that cars are not being shipped out I want to draw the attention of the house to a bill of the preceding government which was passed by parliament this year permitting manufacturers to ship automobiles on consignment to the dealers with the dealers not having to pay excise tax on them until they take title to them after they have made a sale. We were told at that time by the parliamentary assistant to the then minister of finance, and he is still a member of the house, that that was the answer to this problem, that in that way they were going to cure this difficulty. Either they misled the house, misunderstood the legislation or else we are being misled by these hon. gentlemen tonight when they raise this question because that is what we were told last session when this legislation was brought down. It is perfectly possible under that act today to ship cars to any dealer in the country on consignment. The dealer does not take title to them in law until he has arranged his financing, in other words, until he has made his sale, and therefore, according to the words of the parliamentary assistant to the then minister of finance in March of 1957, this problem could be solved very easily.
I do not blame the dealers, Mr. Speaker. The situation goes deeper than that. The fault for this problem, as my hon. friend knows who raised it this afternoon, actually lies with the former government, the government of which he was a distinguished member. That is where the responsibility lies. He told us this afternoon-I do not say boastingly-that his government had reduced the excise tax on automobiles from 25 per cent to 15 per cent and then had reduced it from 15 per cent to 10 per cent. That is perfectly true. But what did they do? They stuck the dealers with the excise tax every time.

We on this side of the house, supported by hon. gentlemen in both corners of the house, urged, pleaded and begged hon. gentlemen opposite when in government to do something about it. They just laughed it off. They said it could not be done and nothing was done. The dealers have made up their minds that they will not be stuck again. It may be that they have forgotten about the consignment act to which I referred a few moments ago but they have been burned twice by our predecessors and they do not realize there is a different government in power which will not stick them again if, as and when reductions are brought in.
In that regard I am in a position to say this. What may be done about reduction of taxation I do not know. It is a matter for the Minister of Finance to make his recommendations to his colleagues in the cabinet and, if approved there, to make his recommendations to parliament and then parliament can approve of them if it sees fit. What his recommendations may be, what they will be, I do not know. But once the recommendations are made it happens to be my responsibility to direct and head up the administration of the Department of National Revenue with its experienced and able officers. I may say, remembering when we sat in opposition and urged the case of the dealers, that I made up my mind that if my colleague the Minister of Finance did reduce the excise tax on automobiles I was not going to be in the position that my predecessor was when he sat here of having to say, "I refuse to do anything for the car dealers."
I was told first that nothing could be done. I asked that the decision be reviewed or considered. I am now satisfied, Mr. Speaker, and I know, after consultation wtih my officers, with the car manufacturers, with the car dealers, the presidents of the associations, the responsible men all across this country, that if-I emphasize again-a tax reduction is made in the excise tax on automobiles, the reduction on that tax will be passed on to the dealers who have cars in their possession at that time. They will not be stuck for them as they have been in the past by preceding governments. So, let us clear this up. Let us get down to facts and realities. Notwithstanding any consignment act or anything else, in the light of the statement I have just made there is no reason why manufacturers cannot start rolling their cars out to dealers tomorrow and have their dealers take possession.
There is nothing further I can say on this matter, Mr. Speaker. I have made the position clear so far as the Department of National Revenue is concerned. Although one cannot get too serious about this, I could not 96698-lllj

Coming as I do from the constituency of Essex West, which comprises chiefly the city of Windsor, that is a great part of the city of Windsor and the township of Sandwich West, I am very vitally concerned with this matter. Unlike the speaker who has just sat down, and who feels he cannot get too serious about this matter, I think it is of very vital concern and one which goes to the very roots of the economic life of the whole of Canada. The automobile industry is not only applicable to those persons who are engaged in the handling and manufacture of automobiles, it goes to all parts of Canada, for most provinces in Canada contribute in some degree towards the manufacturing of automobiles, whether in Windsor, Oakville or Oshawa.
In addition to that, the secondary industries, the feeder plants in various municipalities in Ontario, Quebec, the maritimes and western Canada, are all affected by this matter. It is, therefore, of vital importance. It is something about which we should be most serious. The Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) has posed a question as to whether we have lost faith in Canada. Certainly we have not lost faith in Canada. If we had lost faith in Canada, we would not be here. I hear a few weak voices, but I do not know what they are saying.
However, I shall answer the question as to whether we have lost faith in Canada. We, in the city of Windsor, have absolute confidence, not only in Canada but in ourselves, to play our part in the economic life of this country. All we are looking for is an opportunity to work and an opportunity to help develop this country. We are no alarmists. We are not pessimists, but we do expect co-operation. We expect co-operation from the government. Although the government may not have confidence in itself, we are willing to give them every opportunity of being of assistance, not only to themselves but to the country as a whole.
For that reason the communities in the Windsor area have formed what is known as the metropolitan committee. It is composed

Labour Conditions
of the mayor and reeves of Windsor, Riverside, Tecumseh, Lasalle, Sandwich East township, Sandwich West township, Sandwich South township, St. Clair Beach and Ojibway. Those are the municipalities comprising the Windsor area. They have formed a committee and have looked into the situation. They find there are approximately 12 per cent of the working force at present unemployed. The matter is most acute, and it is most acute to those persons who are primarily and immediately responsible to the public. These people are not in a position at the present time to pay out the large sums that are necessary for carrying these people. They are not able to set up their budgets for the coming year, and therefore find themselves in great difficulty.
Now, to that end, they are most anxious to co-operate with the government. They are most anxious to get the views of the government, so that they may, if at all possible, be of assistance. They are most anxious to do what is possible to help themselves, and to that end they addressed a letter to the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) on November 22, asking that they have an opportunity of interviewing him and discussing the matter with him and with the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Monteith) and the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green). So far there has been no answer to that letter. On November 28, I telephoned to the Prime Minister's office. I talked with his secretary and asked him to look up the letter and let me have a word as quickly as possible when we might be able to see the Prime Minister and the other ministers of the government. So far I have not had a reply by telephone from the Prime Minister's office or the other ministers' offices.
I will say that I did have a personal conversation with the Minister of National Health and Welfare, who was most courteous in trying to arrange this. I, not being satisfied, addressed a letter, because this is a matter of vital urgency to those parts of Canada which I represent, to the Prime Minister asking that he arrange an interview with the Minister of National Health and Welfare and the Minister of Public Works so that this matter could be placed before them by the elected representatives from that area. So far I have not had a reply to that letter, neither have I had a reply from the Minister of National Health and Welfare or the Minister of Public Works. I assume that in due course they will get around to it, and when they do we will be very happy to get their views. If there is anything that we can do to be of assistance we will be most happy to do it.

This matter has created a great deal of concern in the area which I represent, chiefly I think because of the most extravagant promises that were made prior to the last election and which we understand the government is now trying to fulfil.
We wish them well. We hope they can manage all these things. But in the meantime there are things to be done in our part of the country, things which were started by the previous government and which we think should be carried out.
For instance, there is the addition to the new post office which would provide employment in that area. If it had been proceeded with expeditiously, as had been planned by the previous government, all the buildings would now have been demolished and we would be on our way to construction to relieve a large amount of winter unemployment. There are at present in the Windsor area over 9,000 unemployed. It is therefore a very serious matter, one which affects the whole life of the community and the whole life of that part of the province.
I urge you, Mr. Speaker, to try to get some co-operation out of the government. If there is any possible way in which we may be able to be of assistance in helping ourselves, we should like to know about it. But in the meantime, I would appreciate some action by the Prime Minister and his other ministers with regard to seeing a delegation which has been provided by the metropolitan committee in the Windsor area.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise principally to comment on some of the remarks made by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan). I want to start by assuring him that I do not think he is "atrophied in a cocoon". I have known him as an eminent lawyer and as a very competent member of parliament. It is not his intelligence I am going to question but the use he has made of the facts he has at his disposal.
First of all, I wish to congratulate my two colleagues, the hon. members for Essex East (Mr. Martin) and Essex West (Mr. Brown) on taking this parliamentary action in drawing to the attention of parliament and of the country the very serious unemployment occurring in the great motor industry which is centred in their city. It is true that it affects more than the city of Windsor; it affects the other automobile centres of Oshawa, Oakville and Hamilton, but it affects far more than that. It affects every supplier of parts to these great industries right across the country. Every car dealer today has found that his car sales are drying up and he has found it therefore necessary to lay off car salesmen. In my own riding, 3,000 miles from Oshawa and 2,500 miles, I suppose, from Windsor, the car dealers have told me that they are laying off salesmen because nobody is going to buy a car until this situation is cleared up.
I think all of us appreciate the fact that the automobile industry in North America has this problem of recurrent unemployment because of its practice of tuning up annually for new models, and they have to lay off men during that period when new dies are being prepared. The European car manufacturers do not suffer from that problem because they do not change their models as frequently or as completely, and the European car factories have been able to offer more continuous employment than the Canadian or United States manufacturer. It is because of this condition, I think, that the automobile workers union in North America, in both the United States and Canada, have fought so

hard for a guaranteed annual wage in the hope that such action would induce the employers to try to spin the employment out over the whole year instead of working overtime for part of the year and no employment at all for other parts of the year. It is precisely because this great industry has this problem of seasonal unemployment that it is so disastrous when unemployment for other causes is forced on them as well.
The present unemployment without question is due to newspaper stories which have flatly asserted during the past week that there is going to be a tax cut of five per cent in the excise tax. We find these stories across the country and without variation. As my friend, the Minister of National Revenue, pointed out, there is always speculation in this field before the government brings down a budget. The newspapers fly kites which suggest that some taxes are going to go up or come down or no change is going to take place. The members of the opposition fly kites and probe around to see whether they can get some indication from the government what changes are going to be made. The government, of course, is bound by the British tradition and British parliamentary secrecy in budget announcements. And that is why in recent years newspaper speculation has covered the field. Some papers have said that taxes are going to come down; other papers have said that taxes are going to go up, and still other papers say that taxes are going to stay as they are. That is the difference in this situation, because all the papers across the country say that this tax is going to be cut five per cent and it is going to be done in this week. I do not say that there has been a leak anywhere. I think a thing like that would be hard to prove; but certainly there has been some indication given when these reputable gentlemen of the press come to a unanimous decision.
I want to point out to the Minister of National Revenue, however, that this situation today is very different from the situation in any of the 17 years that I have been in parliament or in the 12 years that he has been in parliament. This situation has been caused by the cumulative effect of three separate actions taken by the party which is now the government in this house. And these steps in succession have rightly or wrongly created in the public mind the impression that this excise tax on cars is either going to be reduced or abolished. It is because of that feeling which the public has that car sales have dried up. Naturally, no consumer, with the present high price of cars, is going to pay an unnecessarily high price when he thinks that in a week from

now the price is going to $100 to $200 lower because of tax cuts. And that drying up of sales, of course, backs up on the dealers, which in turn backs up on the car manufacturers.
Let me trace these three steps in order. The first step was the extravagant election promises made by Conservative speakers across the country, and especially by the right honourable gentleman who is now the Prime Minister. He spoke twice on this matter. I have a very fine booklet here which contains the election promises he made to the Canadian people during the last election. He spoke on May 9 in the great automobile city of Windsor. Naturally, on that occasion, according to the press again, he spoke on the automobile taxes. In the press clippings I have of those Windsor speeches he said that this tax was to be reduced. However, he then moved along to Oshawa, another great car centre, and spoke again some three weeks later, on May 29.

John Diefenbaker last night promised that a Conservative government would abolish the excise tax on automobiles and eliminate "in the whole or in the main" all discriminatory excise levies.
The Toronto Telegram, a good Tory sheet, of May 30 had this to say:
He told the automotive town audience his party would lift luxury taxes from cars because they are "an essential part of public and private transportation. There is no more justification for a luxury tax an automobiles than there would have been for one on the horse and buggy 50 years ago."
Then, in the Ottawa Journal, another good Tory sheet, we find the following:
In Oshawa, a city of car production, Mr. Diefenbaker said that if he becomes Prime Minister-
And he is.
-a special fall session of parliament would be called to reduce taxes,-
After seven weeks we have not seen much of that yet but we are still here in session. -including the 10 per cent excise tax on cars which would be removed in whole or in part.
When I reminded the right hon. gentleman of that this afternoon he said that he had been misquoted. I take his word for that.
Labour Conditions

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: No, I did not say "misquoted". I said there was no statement that it would be removed wholly. I have never said that.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I have just read these three accounts of his speeches from very reputable journals. It is from these statements that the people of Canada generally got their information about what the right hon. gentleman was promising, and if these statements in these national journals were inaccurate one would have thought that the Prime Minister or that very great press staff that accompanied him across the country during the last election would have immediately sent corrections to the editors of the Ottawa Journal, the Ottawa Citizen and the Toronto Telegram.
But because no such corrections were made the public, rightly or wrongly, does think that the Prime Minister promised to abolish or at least reduce these excise taxes. I am not going to go into the much larger file I have of the promises of other Conservative condidates. I got one this morning from a correspondent in Huron who pointed out that the whip of the Tory party, the hon. member for Huron (Mr. Cardiff), pledged as well in a public advertisement that the 10 per cent sales tax would be removed, but I do not think the public would place as much importance on his promises as on the statement of the right hon. gentleman. That is the first step. I say these promises have created in the public's mind the feeling today that this excise tax is going to be either abolished or reduced.
The second step which brought about the present unemployment was the budget announcement made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) to Harold Morrison of the Canadian Press on June 25. The Canadian Press is, of course, a co-operative national news gathering service of all the newspapers in this country. The announcement was put on their wires and the next day newspapers from coast to coast carried the first public announcement of the new Minister of Finance promising a fall budget with substantial tax cuts.
The Canadian Press is not the only news gathering group in the country. There is the British United Press as well and there is keen competition between these two services. The British United Press found that it had been scooped when this Canadian Press story appeared in the newspapers of Canada. So one of the representatives of British United Press then had to track down the Minister of Finance, and finally that evening he got him at his hotel. He read the Canadian Press story to him paragraph by paragraph and

Labour Conditions
asked whether each of these statements was true and that night he was told that they were true. So the British United Press as well then sent the story across the country that there was going to be a fall budget with tax cuts. Again the Canadian people, rightly or wrongly, were led to believe that at this session of parliament there would be tax cuts in this luxury tax field which, according to the right hon. gentleman, belonged in the horse and buggy age. That is the second step.
Then there was a third step taken here in this parliament which was the final step in building up this unanimous feeling in the country and in the press that this tax cut is coming and coming this week. Since the opening of parliament members of all three opposition parties, the official opposition, the C.C.F. and the Social Credit, have repeatedly asked the Minister of Finance, when is this budget to come down? Even more so than any handouts people of Canada get through social security legislation they are interested in tax cuts because most of them feel they can spend that money better themselves than any government.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I am now repeating a comment which used to be made at great length by the present Minister of Finance. This again is the question usually asked at the beginning of a session of the minister of finance. I can look across the floor and see half a dozen members who in the past have asked Mr. Ilsley or Mr. Abbott or Mr. Harris, on what date are you going to bring down the budget? Well, early in the session the finance minister would have to say that he did not really know because the work was in progress but as we got along to the end of February and the early part of March he would begin to give some indication. Finally, he would stand up in the house and say, "I am going to present the budget next Thursday night."
But here again the situation is different this session. After our questioning about when the budget was going to be produced and receiving nothing but evasion in reply, evasive denials that these Canadian Press and British United Press interviews ever took place, the opposition members began to doubt if there was going to be a budget. So then we changed our question and asked, not when but is there going to be a budget at all? We got the same long-winded evasive answers, red herrings dragged across our tracks and little sermons on political ethics as well.
Then we asked the Prime Minister directly. After all, he is the head of the government. On November 15 I led off and, together with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and the hon. member for

Acadia (Mr. Quelch), inquired from the Prime Minister whether there was going to be a budget. He referred us to the Minister of Finance. Then, of course, we raised the question of the Minister of Finance having told the nation in this press interview that there was going to be a budget, and on page 1,176 of Hansard of November 15 the Prime Minister answered in this way:
As far as the alleged representation made by the Minister of Finance is concerned-
That is the statement on the budget on June 25.
-my recollection in that regard is that the Minister of Finance has already stated in this house that the statement in question had not been made by him.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Oh, oh!
You will remember that we said much more than "oh, oh". Hon. members who said "oh, oh" will remember that the Minister of Finance was sitting in the next seat to the Prime Minister and he sat there and squirmed and almost got to his feet to explain that he had not said the interview never took place, but nevertheless the matter was allowed to rest at that point.
After seven weeks of tincertainty, today at long last, when the Minister of Finance is absent on other duties, we did learn that there was not going to be a budget. The Prime Minister did tell the house that there was not going to be a budget. The right hon. gentleman and I have been friends since we came to parliament so I know he will not mind if X read back to him a little piece of poetry he read to the house in 1946 during a budget debate when he was criticizing the action or lack of action by our mutual friend, Douglas Abbott, then minister of finance. In view of these three steps, in view of the delay in bringing down a budget or telling us whether or not there was going to be a budget, I think his choice of poetry is particularly appropriate today. Let me read it.
They promise, prepare, propose, postpone.
And end by letting things alone.
No budget! I say, therefore, that the present unusual unemployment in the automobile industry caused by the dry-up of retail sales exists because of these three successive steps; first of all the election promises to reduce or abolish the excise tax on cars which excited public interest and was followed by the statement of the Prime Minister, when he was twitted after the election about these many, many election promises, that these promises-I think I am quoting him correctly-were solemn obligations which will be effectuated. That word "effectuated" drew

my attention so I looked it up in the dictionary and I find that it means what I thought it meant.
So the public had that first of all in their minds. Then they were further excited or further heartened, I suppose, by the further statement of the Minister of Finance to the Canadian Press and to the British United Press four days after having assumed the portfolio that there was going to be a fall budget and there were going to be substantial tax cuts. That certainly confirmed the opinion that the public had formed because of the election promises of the Conservative party.
Then the third step was the evasion in the house of the simple question, first of all, when is there going to be a budget, and then, finally, is there going to be a budget at all, which was finally answered today. It is because of these three steps that we do not have any variation in the press summation of the situation. No papers in Canada tonight are saying that the tax may remain the same or that there may be a 2 per cent, 5 per cent, 8 per cent or 10 per cent reduction. They all say, as the headlines tonight show, that it is going to be a 5 per cent reduction and it is going to come this week.
Well, here in the house today we have learned two things. We have learned from the righteous indignation of the Prime Minister this afternoon that the tax is not going to be abolished so the public can rest assured the tax is not going to be abolished. The Minister of National Revenue when he was speaking either said too little or too much because anyone in this house who listened to him will also be convinced, as the gentlemen of the press were convinced, that the cut is going to be 5 per cent. It is for that reason we find plants closed throughout the country and salesmen laid off.
My hon. friend spoke about the value of the concession made on consignment. It was, of course, not original with his government. It was made by the minister of finance of the previous government. But if he will study his files of correspondence a little more thoroughly he will find that the automotive industry did not think very much of that concession, for two reasons.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: No, but you did.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: If the minister could only have seen the vigour with which he commended this proposal to the house-

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: I was trying to recapture that atmosphere of yours last year.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Let me tell you why the automobile industry does not think very much of this proposal. First of all, the dealers in
habour Conditions
my own riding tell me that automobile manufacturers do not send them many cars on consignment. The manufacturers expect the dealers to pay for the cars. The only way the dealers can avoid receiving the cars is not to take them out of the box cars in the railway yards in Vancouver, and of course that adds to the demurrage. There are some dealers with sufficient influence, apparently, to get cars on consignment but a great many of the dealers do not get cars on consignment. The sale is completed when the car arrives at the show rooms, and they are then beyond tax recovery.
We are not worrying so much about the dealers, it is the possible customer who is thinking of buying that car, we will say in West Vancouver, in my riding. If he buys that car today and the taxes are cut tomorrow he does not get any reduction because the dealer who sold him that car has taken that car and paid the sales tax before he could sell it to the customer. It is these people about whom we are really concerned because it is the drying up of sales to these people that has caused the whole unhappy chain of circumstances leading to the closing of these plants. It is for this reason I say that action should be taken immediately. Whatever elements of secrecy there were about this proposal, they have certainly been washed out by this series of events and by the statements made by both the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and the Minister of National Revenue in this house today.
As the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) and the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) said, this is an action which can be taken instantly by the Minister of Finance, or in his absence by the Prime Minister, by merely putting a notice of motion on the order paper of intention to amend the Excise Tax Act.
We have a little difference in procedure here as compared with the British house. In the British House of Commons when tax changes are notified to the house they have a special statute, a one-year act, which makes these things effective between the date of the announcement and the date of the passage of the necessary act by parliament. Here, by custom, the announcement of the minister in the house, or even on one occasion on the radio, has been sufficient to make these tax changes effective. Naturally, if they are tax cuts no person in the country is going to complain. If they were tax increases, I am informed that a man could hire a lawyer and resist paying these increases until the actual bills have passed in parliament.
These bills, of course, would include a retroactive clause dating back to the

Labour Conditions
announcement of the minister, and once those bills were passed the complaining citizen would be liable for the taxes and interest penalties. It is for that reason I say that all that is needed tomorrow is for the Prime Minister to give notice of his intention of these tax changes, which apparently he has decided and the situation, so far as unemployment caused by the drying up of sales is concerned, will be immediately cured.
If this action took place tomorrow I am sure the plants would start operating the day after and car sales would roll on at the normal rate from that day forward. If the Prime Minister and his government do not choose to take this action, every day of delay means that these many thousands of workers and car salesmen are going to be unemployed and their loss of income will be directly due to the procrastination, stalling and phony promises which have been made in this respect.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I am
sure that the members of this house are probably aware of the fact we do not produce any automobiles in British Columbia. Nevertheless, I think the fact that the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Sinclair), who has just taken his seat, and other members from that province are prepared to show some interest in the discussion we are having is an indication that the situation in the parts of Canada in which they do produce automobiles is one which we feel should be of common concern to all Canadians.
I do not profess to know very much about the intricacies of the production methods followed by automobile companies of Canada, although I do understand that the type of seasonal layoffs to which the hon. member for Coast-Capilano referred some minutes ago are characteristic of that industry and have led, as he described, to periods of seasonal unemployment. However, this particular situation is one that is of more than usual concern to the workers involved. We have heard a good deal of discussion throughout the day of the particular situation that revolves around this question of the possible reduction in excise tax on automobiles. In the lucid style for which he is generally appreciated in this house, the hon. member for Coast-Capilano has given us rather a concise summary of the situation and what has led up to it. Undoubtedly what he says is true that if the announcement which could and should be made is made that will of itself have a considerable effect in reviving production in the automobile industry.
Nevertheless, I think it perhaps is important when we are considering this situation to recognize that if it is this tax situation

which has complicated the layoffs in the automobile industry, when we are thinking of unemployment in the automobile sectors of our economy we must be conscious of the fact that if production is to resume on a scale which would mean full employment there are other related problems which must be considered. As I said at the outset, we do not produce any automobiles in British Columbia. In recent years, however, we have been buying quite a lot of automobiles. I know that the workers in the Comox-Alberni district have been buying quite a few automobiles. I only have to look around me when I am at home to realize that has been the case. I think, therefore, while we are considering this situation in Windsor and the other automobile areas, and while we are discussing this particular tax situation, we should not overlook the general background situation which is closely related to the resumption of full employment in the automobile industry.
I noticed that the Vancouver press, along with the press in other parts of the country, has been carrying stories about the automobile situation, statements by management of the automobile firms that because of the decline in the demand for automobiles they were going to have to cut back their production. However, I think we realize that it is not alone in the automobile industry that such announcements have been taking place. Certainly many of the people on Vancouver island who not many months ago might have been contemplating the purchase of a new automobile this year or next year have not any such ideas in the back of their heads at the present moment and it is not all because of the fact that there is speculation or uncertainty as to the question of an excise tax reduction. A great deal of it is because of the fact that the people who have been working in the production of commodities that we produce in British Columbia are in the same boat as are the automobile workers.
I do not intend to attempt to outline in a barrage of statistics the situation in respect of some of the potential customers for automobiles in British Columbia but figures are coming out which suggest, for example, that there is something in the neighbourhood of a 40 per cent reduction in the over-all production at the present time of our great sawmill industry in British Columbia which means, one could argue, that there are 40 per cent fewer people in the province of British Columbia in that particular industry who are at present potential customers for automobiles. The same thing applies to some of the other related industries. A recent dispatch from one of the British Columbia papers carries an announcement by the management of

Crown Zellerbach Corporation which states that the company's announcement is that they now face the poorest plywood market conditions since the war, proposed to drop 110 employees from their plywood plant on the lower Fraser river; the anticipated production cut is 25 per cent for at least the remainder of the year and possibly longer. That is an announcement coming from the company's side of the picture. On the other hand, I have in my hand a little bulletin that is published by one of the locals of the international woodworkers of America which represents the employees who are engaged in this industry. This bulletin of the Vancouver local of that union has a page here of items of news around the local. Under the heading of "Canadian White Pine" they say:
Lay-offs have caused the majority of problems at the Canadian White Pine. There has been a series of lay-offs at this operation and as a result the whole situation is in a very fluid state.
Dozens of grievances have been filed with the plant committee but most of the grievances have to be changed as a result of further lay-offs.
I imagine that situation is similar to some of the situations about grievances that may have been in process in some of the automobile plants in recent weeks. Then another plant within the jurisdiction of that local, namely Vancouver Plywoods, has this to say:
Main topics of conversation these days has been: 1. The shut-down and general unemployment situation in this industry and others.
Then they go on and describe grievances that arise out of cutbacks which are creating seniority problems in the maintenance and construction sections of the plant. All of these things are, I feel, perhaps closely related to the situation in Windsor and things which should be considered along with the particular matter that sparked this debate when we think of the plight faced by the workers in the automobile industry of Canada at this present time.
The situation in Windsor, I suggest, is very much akin to the situation which has arisen in places like Port Alberni, Courtenay and other centres in my constituency. While we may not have any particular problem in respect of the removal of the excise tax at this time, nevertheless the indications are that as to a fall-off in the demand for some of the products which are produced in British Columbia we have a situation which is similar and one which must be taken into account by the government when it is considering what should be done with regard to creating full employment once again in the automobile industry in the province of Ontario.
I wonder if perhaps this story which is carried on the front page of the last issue of
Labour Conditions
the Vancouver Sun-that is Saturday, November 30-which has reached us here is not indicative of the situation and of the attitude of mind which is developing in some of the areas where these problems of unemployment are arising. Apparently one of the new members of the Conservative party in the House of Commons has been having a little baptism of fire in dealing with this question of unemployment in the city of Vancouver.

speechtext: Order. I must remind the hon. member that we are not dealing with unemployment in general but with unemployment in the automobile industry in particular. speechtext:
I thought I was attempting to indicate that the potential purchasing power of the people of British Columbia was an important factor in the maintenance of employment in the automobile industry in Ontario. While I may have perhaps been giving too much of the background of the situation that is causing a decrease in the potential market for automobiles in British Columbia, nevertheless I felt that it might perhaps be important for me to do it on this occasion. I think it is important that the government of Canada should recognize that these problems which arise in one particular area of the country are, in large part, the result of situations that may be in existence
2,000	or 3,000 miles away and that if they are going to take effective action beyond whatever they may be contemplating doing about this excise tax, certainly it is important that the necessary steps be taken to revive full production in our great forest products industry of British Columbia if the full potential market for cars in Canada is going to be restored to the level which it has reached at previous periods in our economic life.
I was going to suggest that the reaction of unemployed people in Windsor and in Vancouver is inclined to be rather similar. I do not know what the unemployed people down in Windsor are thinking and feeling but apparently the unemployed people of Vancouver expressed themselves rather vigorously when one of the members of parliament from that city apparently showed more interest in the Grey Cup when he raised the subject than he did in the situation which they were up against as unemployed citizens of this country. I certainly agree that the arguments which have been advanced by spokesmen in this group and by spokesmen from the official opposition, and in particular, as I mentioned a few minutes ago, the lucid argument which

Labour Conditions
was presented by the hon. member for Coast -Capilano, are matters which require immediate action and some immediate statement from the government.
I did feel I wanted to spend a little time in bringing to the attention of this house the broad background of this problem and what to me should be even more basic considerations in the minds of the government in approaching the problem raised today by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) than the consideration of an amendment to a particular tax.

As a matter of fact I can only think that what is wanted here is some proof that the member for Algoma East can come before this House of Commons and prove that he, in fact, runs the government and not the party to your right.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Well I see they have awakened once more to your left, sir; they usually do. On the other hand I am greatly concerned that the attitude being displayed is one of despair and of fear. This was particularly brought to my attention by an editorial in a little local newspaper in my own constituency-

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
This editorial is called "Funk Won't Get Us Anywhere!" I was intrigued with the title so I looked up the word "funk" in the dictionary and I found it meant fear or panic. Now the editorial in the Etobicoke Press of Thursday, November 28 among other things says this- and if you feel sir that I should not read this particular article perhaps I can follow the system used in our courts of justice and simply say I would like to adopt these words as my own.
We are not a confirmed optimist-not by any means. But we are seriously concerned about this vicious circle of fear that is prevalent in the thinking of a lot of people today, is reflected in some sections of the dailies, and is having a deleterious effect on the nation as a whole, it seems to us.
Facts are facts and must be faced.
And again:
Over the weekend the fact that Ford lays off 2,400 workers gets the headlines, not the fact that most of them will benefit under the guaranteed annual wage plan (to the tune of half their salary- and that isn't peanuts).

speechtext:
It continues:
You'd think we were in the midst of a depression. We aren't! No one stresses that the government has released $180 million to boost building and has recently stated that it will order the release of further funds for the same purpose if necessary.
No one stresses that Scarborough in September issued $11 million worth of building permits compared with $5,500,000 worth a year ago. No one stresses that in a small municipality like Trafalgar township recently permits were issued for building 77 houses.
No one talks about the new industrial plants that continue to come into Etobicoke and these are only isolated cases!
But the effect of this continued stressing of the bad and no underlining of the good news is this- that the dress manufacturer reads that story in the dailies about middle-class families going without so he immediately plans a smaller output and lays off half his workers. The workers, living close to the collar, can't make their payments on the frig and the car and the washer. These articles are reclaimed by the hundreds and thrown on the

market at half price and the manufacturers of those articles immediately cut down their output staffs and more cars, frigs, washers go for next to nothing.
And all this because of fear-the stressing of the bad only, as we have said.
Give the national economy time-for heaven's sake, for your own sake!
The effect of the $180 million is being felt.
Subdividers are dividing, builders are building houses and factories. And those factories and houses need furniture and hardware and will be occupied by people who will go to the furniture stores and the drug stores and the gas and oil and electric companies for heat and light, and the employees of those companies will in turn be able to keep up their payments on their furniture and cars and whatnot, and people will remain employed and other people will be taken off unemployment and will be able to resume their payments on their articles purchased on time, thus keeping other people in work.
We may be accused of talking without our book, but we think there is a fair modicum of reasoning in what we have pointed out.
Fear creates fear and-well, nothing was ever righted or accomplished through funk!
It seems to me tonight that the chief problem we have to recognize here is that this particular problem in the automobile industry did not arise from a particular question with respect to tax. It arose over a period of time; it arose because, very simply, the opposition to your left while in office did not provide the drive or the dynamic policies required to keep the whole economy on the move. As a matter of fact, if there has been any .problem over the last few years, it has been a problem of laissez faire as far as the opposition to your left is concerned. This country now requires government-

I can only say, if I can come back to what I said earlier today, that if we are going to have a situation arise where, because of reports in the newspaper, it is necessary for the government to disclose immediately all or any of its plans in connection with its fiscal policy, then of course we have abdicated our position of
Labour Conditions
government. If at the same time, because of such reports, corporations are going to be placed in a position where they can say that production shall cease until such time as a definite answer is obtained, then of course we have abdicated in the same way to them.
It seems to me that more than ever it is required that we obey the ordinary rules dealing with disclosure of information of this kind. I cannot help but recall the many times when this arose in the past and we were told very clearly that no information of this type would be given until such time as the government brought down its budget or brought in its budgetary resolutions. I do not think at this time it is a question as to what promises will be kept or not kept. The hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Sinclair) places a great deal of importance on that beautiful red volume which undoubtedly will get a lot of reading, but I should like to say to him tonight that I feel confident that if he is going to prepare another volume in which to include the promises which have been kept then he will, I am sure, have just as large a volume or maybe a larger one.
As I said, this is not a question of keeping promises. The promises which this party gave in its campaign are being kept to a larger extent than ever before, and I am sure that this will continue down to any promises made to people in this or any other industry, but the issue at stake tonight is whether we should abdicate our powers either to the press or to the industry concerned, neither of which I am prepared to do. And I think we can go one step further and say that we have no intention of abdicating our power to the party on your left, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I be allowed to say a few words on this matter. It is a very important one since it affects not only the automobile industry but various other related industries. I believe that the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) was well advised to raise this question so that the people of this country may be made aware of what course the government should be taking after the promises it made in this regard.
A moment ago I was listening to the hon. member for York West (Mr. Hamilton). He reminded me of a familiar French song which says: "Everything has burned down, the stable and the horses too, but everything is just fine, Madame la marquise!" Frankly, the situation being what it is, we wonder what the government can be thinking about at this time.

Labour Conditions
It has just been said that this situation has nothing to do with the promises made by the Conservatives. But had the member for York West taken the trouble to analyse the speech made by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Sinclair) he would have understood without any difficulty that this situation has not been brought about, essentially, by the fact that the press has reported statements made by the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) during the elections, nor those of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) who, during the Prime Minister's stay in England, has continued, day after day, to make repeated statements calculated to convince those who heard them that Canada was to become prosperous overnight because the Conservative party was again in power. What is happening now is the outcome of the unrest caused in this country by the Conservative party in making promises it is in no position to implement, and which it has no intention of carrying out. And yet, today, we are told that is the fault of the Liberal party which has just been turned out of office.
Well, Mr. Speaker, in 1930 we realized that the promises of the Conservative party and of the then prime minister had caused the depression we underwent at that time.
Besides what the hon. member for Coast-Capilano said, the Prime Minister's statements about diverting to the United Kingdom 15 per cent of Canada's trade with the United States have caused uneasiness in the area of Windsor and surrounding cities where the automobile industry is the main employer of the people.
Well, Mr. Speaker, time has come for the Conservative party to remember its promises and to put an end to all those rumours which are left circulating without ever being confirmed. As already said by some members, if the Conservative party really intends to put an end to the present situation in the automobile industry, all it would have to do would be to say whether or not it proposes to change the situation existing at this time as regard taxes. The automobile industry, and the related industries, would then resume their activities and the workers would go back to their jobs.
We should not forget that, when there is unrest in one part of the country, it is felt in the rest of the country. It is like the human body; if one arm is aching, the rest of the body feels it. Since we are at the stage where we are suffering from extraordinary uneasiness and unrest, the Conservative party now directing the destinies of this country should pull itself together and take steps to remedy the situation. That is what we have been requesting all day and
that is also what we intend to continue urging upon the government. Let the Conservative party keep the promises it has made to the Canadian people.

1.	Does the government pay compensation for cattle discovered to have t.b.? If so, what amount is paid per head?
2.	How does the government determine what cattle have t.b.?
3.	Are any veterinarians employed by the dominion government for the purpose of inspecting cattle to determine whether or not cattle have t.b.? If so, how many are thus employed and where?
Answer by: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister of
Agriculture):
1.	Yes, when such cattle react to a tuberculin test under the terms of the restricted area and accredited herd plans. The Animal Contagious Diseases Act provides that compensation shall not exceed $100 each for purebred animals and $40 each for grade animals. In addition the owner receives the commercial market value for his animals at the time of slaughter in an inspected abattoir.
2.	By the application of the intradermal tuberculin test.
3.	Two hundred and fourteen full time salaried veterinary officers are engaged by this department in field disease control and part of their duties is the tuberculin testing of cattle. In addition to the full time salaried officers, there are 170 practising veterinarians employed on a part time basis.
